title: Sacramentals (CCC 1667–1673)
hook: holy water, blessings, medals, ashes: signs that prepare us for grace

segments.voice: Yesterday, the domestic church: the home as a little church, and the Church as a home for everyone. Your line was a little church. Did you keep your small moment? Day one thousand one hundred nine.

Registration, napkins, a tire gauge, and, at the back of a glove box opened at a gas station, a small medal of Saint Christopher on a chain, gone dull. Nobody remembers who put it there. On a windowsill at home, a plastic bottle shaped like the Virgin Mary, half full of water. A farmer asks a priest to bless his tractor. On Ash Wednesday, strangers on a subway car share the same gray smudge. None of these is a sacrament. All of them are something, and the Catechism has a word for that something. It's today's word.
screen: `A MEDAL IN THE GLOVE BOX.` → `WATER IN A BOTTLE ON THE SILL.` → `A GRAY SMUDGE ON A FOREHEAD.`

segments.voice: Sacramentals, the Catechism says, are sacred signs that bear a likeness to the sacraments. Holy water, blessings, medals, ashes, the sign of the cross, a blessed candle. The difference matters. Catholic teaching holds that the sacraments were instituted by Christ and give grace through the action itself. Sacramentals were instituted by the Church. They don't give grace the way a sacrament does. Instead, the Catechism says, they prepare a person to receive grace and to cooperate with it. They work through the prayer of the Church. They clear the ground. A sacramental takes an ordinary moment, walking into a building, starting a car, falling asleep, and opens it toward God. The Catechism says that for well-disposed believers, almost every event of life can be made holy this way. Among sacramentals, blessings come first. Scripture has them too. In Numbers, God gives Aaron's family words to bless the people with. In the Douay-Rheims they begin: "The Lord bless thee, and keep thee." Blessings of people, of meals, of objects, of places. And here's a detail worth keeping: the Catechism says every baptized person is called to be a blessing, and to bless. Some blessings belong to bishops and priests, but parents can bless their children, and a family can bless its table. One more thing the Catechism keeps clear. The power isn't in the water or the metal by itself. A medal isn't a charm. It works, Catholic teaching says, through the Church's prayer and the faith of the person who uses it. Small holy things, pointing past themselves.
screen: `SIGNS THAT RESEMBLE THE SACRAMENTS.` · `THEY PREPARE FOR GRACE.` · `THE LORD BLESS THEE, AND KEEP THEE.` · `NOT A CHARM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bless yourself with holy water. If you have holy water at home, or you're near a church, dip your fingers and make the sign of the cross slowly, forehead, chest, left shoulder, right. If you don't, the slow sign of the cross alone, or simply resting your hand on your heart, can mark the moment. Then settle, and breathe. Notice where your hand traveled. Let one ordinary part of your day come to mind, the drive, the desk, the dishes, and picture it marked the same way. The bell holds the time.
Sacramental. A sacred sign instituted by the Church, like holy water, a blessing, a medal or ashes, that prepares a person to receive grace, working through the Church's prayer. Today's word.
Your line: small holy things. Today, notice one small sign in your day, a cross, a candle, a word of blessing, and let it point past itself. Day one thousand one hundred nine.

howItsDone: Catholics bless themselves with holy water on entering a church, wear blessed medals or scapulars, receive ashes on Ash Wednesday, and ask priests to bless homes, objects and people.
